chunks: Abū ‘Abdil Raḥmān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥusain Al-‘Askari narrated to me from Ḥasan ibn ‘Ali ibn Mahziyār, from his father ‘Ali ibn Mahziyār, from ‘Ali ibn Ḥusain ibn ‘Ali ibn ‘Umar ibn ‘Ali ibn Ḥusain ibn ‘Ali ibn Abī Ťālib, from ‘Ali ibn Ja’far ibn Muḥammad, from his brother Abil Ḥasan Mūsā ibn Ja’far, from his father, from his grandfather (peace be upon him), who said:

‘Ali ibn Ḥusain (peace be upon him) used to stand by the grave of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), say Salām, and testify that he conveyed the message. Then he would supplicate with whatever came to his mind. Thereafter, he would lean his back against the grave of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), against the green marble that is narrow and attached to the side of the grave. He would lean his back against the grave, face the Qiblah,

and say: 'O Allāh! To You I entrust my affair, and to the grave of Muḥammad (peace be upon him), Your slave and Your messenger, I have leaned my back. And to the Qiblah that You approved for Muḥammad (peace be upon him), I have turned my face. O Allāh! I have become in the morning unable to secure for myself any of the good that I hope for, nor to avert from myself any of the harm that I fear. And all affairs are in Your Hand. And there is no one more needy than I. I am in need of the good that You have sent down to me. O Allāh! Grant me a return from You with goodness, for there is none who can withhold Your grace. O Allāh! I seek refuge in You from You changing my name, or altering my body, or removing Your blessing from me. O Allāh! Adorn me with piety, beautify me with blessings, grant me a long healthy life, and provide me with gratitude for that health.'
ai.seo_question: What is the specific supplication recited by Imam Sajjad (a.s.) when leaning against the Prophet's grave?
ai.summary: This narration from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* highlights the devotional practice of Imam Zayn al-Abidin, who would lean his back against the Prophet’s grave (specifically the *Marmarah*) while facing the Qiblah, symbolizing reliance on the Prophet as an intercessor and a spiritual anchor. The supplication emphasizes human fragility and the need for divine preservation of one’s identity and blessings, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the grave as a locus of spiritual connection (*wasilah*) rather than mere veneration.
